title: Job 21:1–16
context: Job, replying to Zophar, asks the friends to listen and then mock if they will, and turns to what horrifies him: the wicked often live long, grow powerful, see their children established, and go down to the grave in peace. He reports their own words to God, “Depart from us,” and their question, “What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” Job’s challenge to the friends’ retribution scheme stands as real, and both traditions share the observation that the wicked can prosper for a time (cf. Ps 73:3; Jer 12:1) while God remains just.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Job answered.” Arminian readers note that Job now replies directly to Zophar’s claims about the wicked.

In this speech he answers the friends’ argument about the wicked point by point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job turning from lament to sustained argument.

Shared ground: both traditions name Job as the speaker and read his words as a real challenge within the debate, not as a lapse to be quickly corrected.

verses.text: “Listen diligently to my speech. Let this be your consolation.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Listen diligently to my speech. Let this be your consolation.” Arminian readers note that Job asks only to be heard.

Listening would be more comforting than their speeches.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a pastoral lesson in Job’s request.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that attentive listening is often the first act of comfort for those who suffer.

verses.text: Allow me, and I also will speak. After I have spoken, mock on.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Allow me, and I also will speak. After I have spoken, mock on.” Arminian readers note Job’s frustration with the friends’ scorn.

He expects to be mocked but insists on speaking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job’s determination to be heard despite their contempt.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an honest expression of Job’s distress, not as rebellion.

verses.text: As for me, is my complaint to man? Why shouldn’t I be impatient?
verses.arminianNotes:
“As for me, is my complaint to man? Why shouldn’t I be impatient?” Arminian readers note that Job’s complaint is directed toward God, not merely toward the friends.

He explains his impatience by the depth of his trouble.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job bringing his complaint before God.

Shared ground: both traditions see lament addressed to God as part of faith (cf. Ps 13:1–2), even when it is raw.

verses.text: Look at me, and be astonished. Lay your hand on your mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Look at me, and be astonished. Lay your hand on your mouth.” Arminian readers note that Job invites the friends to be silenced by his condition.

His suffering should give them pause.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a call for humility in the face of mystery.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Job will later lay his own hand on his mouth before the LORD (40:4), which they read as a related but distinct moment.

verses.text: When I remember, I am troubled. Horror takes hold of my flesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When I remember, I am troubled. Horror takes hold of my flesh.” Arminian readers note that what follows troubles Job deeply.

He does not raise the problem of the wicked lightly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the anguish behind Job’s question.

Shared ground: both traditions read Job’s horror with compassion, recognizing that questions about God’s justice can shake the faithful.

verses.text: “Why do the wicked live, become old, yes, and grow mighty in power?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why do the wicked live, become old, yes, and grow mighty in power?” Arminian readers note that Job directly contradicts Zophar’s claim that their triumph is short (20:5).

Jeremiah asks a similar question (Jer 12:1).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take Job’s question as a real one that Scripture itself raises (cf. Ps 73:3, 12).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the wicked sometimes prosper and that this troubles the faithful, and they let the question stand.

verses.text: Their child is established with them in their sight, their offspring before their eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their child is established with them in their sight, their offspring before their eyes.” Arminian readers note the painful contrast with Job, whose children have died.

The wicked enjoy what Job has lost.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the sharpness of Job’s observation.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion, recognizing Job’s grief behind his argument, and both note that it answers Zophar’s claim in 20:10.

verses.text: Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them.” Arminian readers note that Job sees no sign of God’s discipline on the wicked.

This contradicts the friends’ scheme.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job’s honest observation of the world.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that outward circumstances do not reliably show who is righteous, and both let Job’s challenge stand here.

verses.text: Their bulls breed without fail. Their cows calve, and don’t miscarry.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their bulls breed without fail. Their cows calve, and don’t miscarry.” Arminian readers note the picture of agricultural prosperity.

Job had lost his own herds (1:14–17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the outward blessing that the wicked appear to enjoy.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God gives good gifts even to the unrighteous (cf. Matt 5:45), which complicates any simple reading of prosperity.

verses.text: They send out their little ones like a flock. Their children dance.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They send out their little ones like a flock. Their children dance.” Arminian readers note the image of joyful family life.

The contrast with Job’s loss is sharp.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the poignancy of Job’s description.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s honest account of what he sees, written with grief rather than envy.

verses.text: They sing to the tambourine and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They sing to the tambourine and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.” Arminian readers note the celebration in the homes of the wicked.

Their lives are filled with music.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the joy that the wicked appear to have.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Job’s own “harp” has turned to mourning (30:31), and both read this verse as part of his challenge.

verses.text: They spend their days in prosperity. In an instant they go down to Sheol.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They spend their days in prosperity. In an instant they go down to Sheol.” Arminian readers note that even their death seems easy.

They do not suffer a lingering end.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job observing that the wicked can die without visible judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the timing of death is not a reliable verdict on a life, and they let the observation stand.

verses.text: They tell God, ‘Depart from us, for we don’t want to know about your ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job reports what the wicked say to God: “Depart from us, for we don’t want to know about your ways.” Arminian readers note that these are the words of the wicked, not Job’s own.

Eliphaz later attributes similar words to the wicked (22:17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise attribute the speech to the wicked whom Job describes.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse carefully as reported speech, showing the open rejection of God that still prospers in Job’s observation.

verses.text: What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? What profit should we have, if we pray to him?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The wicked ask, “What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? What profit should we have, if we pray to him?” Arminian readers note that Job is reporting their words, not adopting them.

Malachi 3:14 records a similar complaint.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the question as the voice of the wicked within Job’s speech.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, noting that Job himself continues to address God throughout the book even in his complaint.

verses.text: Behold, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the wicked is far from me.” Arminian readers note that Job distances himself from the wicked even while describing their success.

Eliphaz uses the same words in 22:18.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Job refusing to join the wicked.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s affirmation that prosperity is in God’s hands, though the exact sense of the first line is discussed.
